metadata.title: Attorney Matthew Skiba Targets Democrats in Politicized Investigation

existing_copy_for_context_only.short: Attorney Matthew Skiba Targets Democrats in Politicized Investigation
existing_copy_for_context_only.medium: Attorney Matthew Skiba has been involved in a politicized investigation targeting Democrats, including a Democratic political consulting firm with ties to Judge Juan Merchan, who presided over Trump's hush payment fraud case. The investigation has been criticized as an abuse of power and an attempt to intimidate political opponents.
existing_copy_for_context_only.long: An August 2026 Emptywheel post connected federal prosecutor Matthew Skiba to a subpoena investigation involving a Democratic political consulting firm with ties to Judge Juan Merchan, who presided over Donald Trump’s New York criminal case. The post also described prosecutor William Hogan’s role in a separate case involving the Broadview Six, a group of immigration protesters; that prosecution was withdrawn after Judge April Perry questioned prosecutors’ conduct before a grand jury. Emptywheel argued that the subpoena investigation was politically retaliatory and connected it to Merchan’s family. That is the author’s interpretation, not an official finding that Skiba targeted Democrats to punish the judge. The supplied record does not name the consulting firm, reproduce the subpoena, explain what records investigators sought, or include responses from the prosecutors or the U.S. attorney. existing_copy_for_context_only.medium: Donald Trump's use of his presidency to increase his personal wealth has raised concerns among legal and ethics experts. Trump has earned an 'unprecedented' $2.2 billion in income during his second term, and his crypto, airplane, and other business ventures have been accused of violating the emoluments clause. The clause prohibits federal officials from accepting gifts or payments from foreign governments.
existing_copy_for_context_only.long: A 2026 Slate legal Q&A considers a listener’s question about whether Trump’s crypto, airplane and other business ventures could violate the Constitution’s emoluments clauses. The writers distinguish the Foreign Emoluments Clause, which bars federal officials from accepting certain gifts or payments from foreign states without congressional consent, from the Domestic Emoluments Clause, which limits the president to a fixed salary and bars additional benefits from the federal government or states. The piece discusses how those provisions might apply when a president’s private businesses receive payments while he is in office. It is legal commentary posing an open question, not a court ruling that Trump violated either clause. The Slate discussion does not provide a calculation supporting the preserved medium’s $2.2 billion income figure or identify how that total was derived.
